title: When AI Makes Things Up
hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.
key_points: A hallucination is AI stating something false as if it were fact.
It happens because models predict plausible text, not verified truth.
The danger is the confident tone — wrong answers sound just like right ones.
Defend yourself: verify facts, ask for sources, and check anything that matters.
content_html: When an AI confidently tells you something that simply isn't true — a fake quote, a made-up statistic, a book that doesn't exist — that's called a hallucination. It's tempting to think of it as a bug, but it's actually the technology behaving exactly as built. A generative model's whole job is to produce text that sounds right based on patterns it has seen. Most of the time plausible and true line up. Sometimes they don't, and the model produces a plausible falsehood with the same fluent confidence.
extra_html: That confidence is the real hazard. A wrong answer doesn't come with a warning label or a nervous tone — it reads exactly like a correct one. People have submitted legal documents citing court cases the AI invented, and trusted summaries that quietly got the facts wrong. The fix isn't to distrust AI entirely; it's to use it for what it's good at and verify the rest. Treat any specific fact, name, date, number, or citation as unconfirmed until checked. Ask the model for its sources and then actually look them up. For anything that carries real consequences — medical, legal, financial — AI is a starting point, never the final word.

related.title: Generative AI
related.hook: The AI behind ChatGPT and image generators doesn't look up answers — it predicts what plausibly comes next, one piece at a time, until it has built a whole response.

related.title: Chatbots & Assistants
related.hook: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini feel like talking to a person, but they're generative AI with a chat wrapper — brilliant writing partners, unreliable encyclopedias.

related.title: Using AI Responsibly
related.hook: The point of AI literacy isn't to use AI for everything — it's to use it well: check its work, be honest that you used it, and know the moments to put it down.

related.title: How to Fact-Check AI
related.hook: You can't tell a true AI answer from a made-up one by reading it — both sound equally sure. So build a habit: for anything that matters, verify it somewhere that isn't the AI.

related.title: What AI Can't Do
related.hook: Today's AI can write a sonnet and flunk a question a child gets right. Knowing its hard edges — no real understanding, no live truth, no common sense — is what makes you good at using it.

flashcards.prompt: Why do AI chatbots 'hallucinate' false information?

choices.text: They predict plausible-sounding text, not verified truth

flashcards.explanation_html: A generative model produces what sounds right based on patterns. With no fact-checker inside, a plausible-sounding falsehood can come out the same way.

flashcards.back_html: The confident tone. A made-up answer is delivered just as fluently as a correct one, so you can't tell them apart without checking.

flashcards.prompt: What's the best defense against AI hallucinations?

choices.text: Independently verify facts, names, and numbers that matter
Ask the same question twice and trust the second answer
Assume longer answers are more accurate

flashcards.explanation_html: Verification is the only reliable defense — check sources and cross-check anything important; repetition and length don't signal accuracy.
